title: Twelve Consoles, One Investigation
thesis: The bottleneck in alert investigation is not model intelligence but the disconnect between a dozen consoles, so a read-only harness that sits on top of existing tools, cites every claim and leaves decisions to people can investigate even low-severity alerts thoroughly in minutes.
summary: Iqbal opens with a fictional low-severity alert: a VPN login from a rarely seen country that succeeded, fired three times in the same second. He says answering whether the login is legitimate means pivoting across twelve consoles (SIEM, identity provider, SaaS security, web gateway, threat intel, MDM, device trust, asset inventory, CAASM, email security, HR and travel approvals), which takes 30 to 60 minutes and is not done for low alerts, and that different analysts investigate differently. He presents Ultron, a read-only investigation harness built by merging two earlier projects, Alfred (plumbing: manifest, installer, secrets guard, permission rules, CI) and Friday (case-review loop and forensic drivers, built with an ex-cyber law enforcement investigator). Ultron runs a tick every 10 minutes: it takes a lease, pulls up to five cases, checks that every data source is alive, then starts one sub-agent per case that follows a canonical playbook, weighs two hypotheses, builds a timeline and tries to disprove itself. Routing is by playbook first, otherwise by indicator type, and new indicators are routed again. The trust model is read-only by construction (GET-pinned drivers, no write tools in the toolset, CI blocks additions), an ask tier that denies after two minutes of silence, and mandatory citation of every claim. A replayed fictional case shows network, device and physical-plane evidence combining to show the real user was working from Latveria behind a travel-router tunnel, in about four minutes. He closes on human accountability: Ultron produces evidence and a likelihood, and HR and a manager make the call.
argument: Security teams have enough tools but lack the connective layer, so answering one question about one low alert requires about twelve logins, query languages and timestamp formats and 30 to 60 minutes, which means low alerts get a glance and investigation quality varies by analyst.
A harness that sits on top of the existing tools, runs on a timer and follows one canonical playbook standardizes investigations and covers every alert, including low ones.

The harness is safe to give access to security tools because it is read-only by construction (write tools are absent from the toolset, not forbidden by prompt), asks a human outside its allowed line, and must cite a query result for every claim.
No single plane of evidence settles a location question because network egress can be bought or spoofed; network, device and physical-plane evidence together produce a verdict.
Even a high-likelihood result is not a verdict on a person: the system supplies cited facts and humans interview, decide and own the outcome.

claims.claim: Investigating one low alert by hand across twelve consoles takes roughly 30 to 60 minutes, so teams do not do it thoroughly for low-severity alerts.
claims.evidence: Walkthrough of the pivots on a fictional alert; slide lists 12 logins, 12 query languages, 12 timestamp formats, 30 to 60 minutes per alert.

claims.claim: A Cisco study from before the AI boom found that 44 percent of security alerts are not investigated, and the figure has likely grown.
claims.evidence: Cited from memory with no link; the statement that the figure has grown is the speaker's inference.

claims.claim: Ultron runs a tick every 10 minutes, takes an execution lease, picks at most five cases from the SIEM, and checks source health before any query so that an empty result is not confused with a dead log source.
claims.evidence: Architecture slide and speaker description; slide shows query window of cursor minus 5 minutes and a heartbeat alert after 35 minutes.

claims.claim: Each case gets its own isolated sub-agent that follows a canonical playbook, holds two competing hypotheses, builds a UTC timeline against baselines, tries to disprove its own theory, and labels findings CONFIRMED, DEDUCED or UNKNOWN.
claims.evidence: Architecture slide and replayed terminal demo showing H1 (really in Latveria, US presence is a tunnel) versus H2 (benign).

claims.claim: Read-only is enforced by construction: every connector sits behind a GET-pinned chokepoint, isolate, change-case and disable-account tools are not in the toolset, and CI fails the build if one is added.
claims.evidence: Stated design plus trust-boundary slide; no test results or bypass attempts shown.

claims.claim: Any action outside the allow or deny rules goes to an ask tier, such as reading data off the laptop, and an unanswered prompt is treated as no after two minutes.
claims.evidence: Stated design; slide says unattended prompt equals denied.

claims.claim: Every claim in the report must cite its query result, the query and the data, and a verification pass drops anything uncited.
claims.evidence: Stated design with a trust-boundary slide: no citation, no claim.

claims.claim: In the replayed case the harness reached a high-likelihood verdict in about four minutes versus 30 to 60 minutes by hand.
claims.evidence: Replay of a fictional case, with the slide stating roughly four minutes; no real-incident timing or sample of cases.

claims.claim: A VPN leak was exposed by 10 seconds of Latveria residential traffic in 90 days of Texas residential connections (41,882 connections), corroborated by a travel router upstream of the laptop, a time zone forced to US, Wi-Fi regulatory country code XL, and a 140 ms latency floor where a US path would be under 30 ms.
claims.evidence: Evidence table and network timeline slides from the fictional replay, each row tiered SPOOFABLE or CONFIRMED.

claims.claim: Network egress alone never settles location: a hosting, anonymizer or bought residential IP is treated as UNKNOWN and the investigation moves to the physical plane.
claims.evidence: Routing rule 4 on the routing slide and the case walkthrough.

claims.claim: New models are evaluated by back-testing on stored known cases and playbooks, and a model is questioned if it does not reproduce known results or is too expensive for the case type.
claims.evidence: Answer in Q&A; no results given.

claims.claim: Analyst-correction count is the feedback signal for false positives and negatives, and changes reach production only through a pull request reviewed by teammates; a weekly scorecard compares the harness to analysts.
claims.evidence: Q&A answer plus trust-boundary slide item 4.

frameworks.name: Ultron tick architecture
frameworks.description: Operator (start and cancel commands, cron heartbeat) leads to a tick every 10 minutes (lease, load state, query cases since cursor minus 5 minutes, pick up to 5, source-health preflight), then an investigation core (one sub-agent per case, canonical playbook, H1 versus H2, UTC timeline, baselines, CONFIRMED/DEDUCED/UNKNOWN), then an evidence bus (MCP servers and GET-pinned drivers ranked by information gain). Local state holds a case tracker, alert memory (hints, never evidence), a scorecard, a 30-day investigation graph and an append-only log. Human-gated: on-box reads use the ask rule, write and containment tools are absent, an unattended prompt is denied.

frameworks.name: Indicator-based routing
frameworks.description: Match a playbook first (account takeover, phishing, insider geo-fraud, malware, exfiltration, offboarding, cloud); otherwise route by indicator: IP, domain or URL to web gateway and threat intel; user to identity provider and HR and travel approvals; host, process or file to EDR, MDM and asset inventory; email to email security; physical location to an ask-gated on-device read. Each new indicator is routed again, which is how the investigation crosses planes. Egress never settles location.

frameworks.name: Trust boundary (four guardrails)
frameworks.description: 1. Read-only by construction, not by instruction, with CI failing if a write tool is added. 2. Outside the line, ask a human, and no answer means no. 3. Every claim cites a query result. 4. Scored against analysts, cheap when idle: weekly scorecard, a quick pre-check, and the full investigation only when a case changed.

frameworks.name: Evidence tiers by plane
frameworks.description: Evidence is classed SPOOFABLE (network egress) or CONFIRMED (sign-in time pattern, device state, HR context, travel router, forced time zone, Wi-Fi regulatory code, latency floor) and organized into network, device and physical planes; no single plane proves a location claim.

frameworks.name: Alfred and Friday merge
frameworks.description: Alfred is the spine: one manifest declaring every agent, skill and connector, an installer wiring them into the AI runtime, shared runtime with central secrets and permission rules, schema checks and CI. Friday is the brain: automated case-review loop, read-only forensic drivers one per system, human-approved on-device geolocation checks, evidence tiers and a structured incident report. Alfred's gap was not knowing how to investigate; Friday's gap was three drifting copies of how to investigate a case.

slide_only: The fictional alert card: user corp\javery, host javery-EX7Q2K4MXC, country Latveria, source IP 203.0.113.57, result SUCCESS, not seen in the last 30 days; three LOW alerts fired in the same second: a user connected to a VPN from a suspicious country, first successful VPN access from a country in org, unusual VPN access from ASN.

The twelve-console diagram grouped as 1 alert (SIEM), 2 identity (identity provider, SaaS security), 3 network (web gateway, threat intel), 4 device (MDM, device trust, asset inventory, CAASM), 5 email if you are paranoid (email security), 6 people (HR system, travel authorization), with the footer 12 logins, 12 query languages, 12 timestamp formats, 30 to 60 minutes per alert.

Ultron harness slide: sits on top of the tools you already have; does the analyst's legwork; runs every 10 minutes and investigates even LOW cases; hands a human an evidence-backed answer, can look at everything, changes nothing.

Merge slide chips: 1 manifest as source of truth, 1 canonical investigation playbook, read-only drivers behind 1 GET-only chokepoint, 10-minute case-review loop, every claim cites evidence, write tools not in toolset, CI containment test.

Tick slide details: operator commands /ultron start|cancel, cron heartbeat, alert at more than 35 minutes; local state files case-tracker.json (cursor, 72 h dedupe), alert_memory.json (hint, never evidence), scorecard.json, investigation-graph (30 d), append-only log; full reference drawing said to be in the appendix.

Terminal replay transcript: preflight.sources shows identity, endpoint and network ok with lags of 42s, 18s and 55s, hr and intel ok; network.egress_history for 90 days shows 198.51.100.23 ASN 64500 residential Dallas US 41,882 conns and 203.0.113.57 ASN 64501 residential Latveria 3 conns 10 s; side panel tracks hypotheses H1 and H2, evidence chips (network, identity, endpoint, HR, intel, on-box) and verdict pending; footer shows write actions 0 and says fictional example, names, IPs and IDs invented.
Timeline slide: Dallas line until 09:11:38, Latveria blip 09:11:46 to 09:11:56, back to US at 09:11:57, on 2026-03-14 UTC.

Evidence table rows with tiers: network egress one Texas home line for 90 days (SPOOFABLE); network sign-ins peak 04:00 US equals 11:00 in Latveria (CONFIRMED); device no VPN client and no tunnel adapter; HR no approved international work; physical gateway travel router upstream of the laptop; time zone forced to US by hand with auto time zone off; Wi-Fi regulatory country code XL (after approval) says Latveria; latency 140 ms floor versus under 30 ms for a US path. Caption: no single plane proves it, network plus device plus physical together do.

Masking diagram: work laptop with no VPN installed connected by Ethernet to a travel router that holds the VPN, an always-on encrypted tunnel of about 9,000 km and about 140 ms round trip to a home in Dallas acting as VPN endpoint or relay on a residential IP, then to the office network that sees a Texas home IP; when the tunnel drops for seconds the real Latveria IP leaks.

Human-element slide: four steps evidence package, analyst review, interview (HR and manager meet the employee), decision (HR and Legal decide outcome and access changes); data cannot see context such as relocation in progress, an approval that never reached the system, a family emergency.
Final slide: right user yes, right place no; the real user, not a threat actor, masking that they are in Latveria; Ultron proved it in about four minutes.
demos: Replay of a fictional case in a terminal UI (ultron tick, case CASE-10427): clusters three LOW alerts into one case, runs a source-health preflight, states two hypotheses, queries 90-day egress history and finds the 10-second Latveria connection, then (per the speaker) walks the remaining systems and the physical plane after an analyst approves the on-device read, ending with a cited high-likelihood verdict in about four minutes. The video was embedded and the speaker narrated; only the first part is legible in the recording.

offense: VPN-masked remote work: a hardware travel router holds an always-on tunnel to a home relay on a residential IP, so the laptop has no VPN software and endpoint tooling looks clean while the office sees a domestic residential IP.
Concealment signals: forcing the laptop time zone to a US value and disabling automatic time zone to hide local time.
Residential IPs can be purchased, so IP geolocation and threat-intel reputation are spoofable and cannot answer where a user physically is.
Failure mode on the defender side: an empty query result and a dead log source look identical unless source health is verified.
defense: Run a source-health preflight before every investigation so that an empty result is trusted only when the log source is reporting.

Build agent access read-only by construction: pin connectors to GET, leave isolate, change-case and disable-account tools out of the toolset, and add a CI containment test that fails when a write tool appears.
Put a human-ask tier around sensitive reads (for example on-device reads) and default to deny on timeout so unattended runs are safe.
Require every claim in an agent report to cite its query, result and data, and drop uncited claims in a verification pass.
Route by playbook, then by indicator type, rather than running every tool on every case, and re-route on each new indicator.
Treat network egress as spoofable; corroborate location with device state, travel-router or gateway evidence, Wi-Fi regulatory domain and a latency floor from traceroute.
Back-test new models on stored known cases before adopting them, batch cases to avoid cost blowouts from alert storms, and gate changes through pull requests.
takeaways: The talk's support is one fictional replay, so treat this as a test to run: count how many consoles and query languages your analysts cross for a low alert, and if the answer is around a dozen, check whether a read-only harness over existing tools buys more coverage than a new detection tool.

If you give an agent security-tool access, remove write and containment tools from its toolset and test for that in CI, rather than relying on prompt instructions. The talk shows no bypass tests, so verify the design before trusting it.
Make agent reports auditable by requiring a cited query result per claim and discarding the rest. The talk shows no measured effect, so check that the verification pass really drops uncited claims.
Add a source-health check to automated investigations so empty results are not read as clean.
Keep verdicts about people with humans: have the agent output likelihood plus evidence and route to analyst review, then HR or Legal.
limits: Ultron is read-only today; the speaker said he would still keep a human in the loop for likely true positives and consider fully autonomous handling only where confidence is near 100 percent, such as false positives.
Scaling is bounded by batch size to avoid an alert storm of false positives blowing the budget.
The 10-second network blip alone is a lead, not proof.
critique: No production numbers were given: no count of alerts or cases handled, precision or recall, false-positive rate, cost per investigation, or comparison against analyst verdicts; the four-minute figure is from a replayed fictional case.
The main case is a fictional replay, so it shows the design working on a prepared example; it does not show how often the harness finds such cases or how it behaves on real ones.
The 44 percent Cisco statistic was cited from memory without a title or link, and the statement that the figure has grown is the speaker's inference.
The read-only claim rests on GET-pinned drivers, but GET is not guaranteed side-effect free on every API, and no test results or bypass attempts were shown.
The back-testing and scorecard statements were made in Q&A and no results were shown; the number of analyst corrections measures analyst intervention rather than accuracy directly.
qa: How did you come up with the processes fed to the harness? Answer: he worked with an ex-cyber law enforcement officer; they wrote each playbook as a file listing the steps for a case type, the false positives to rule out and how to reach a verdict; unmatched cases get broader querying.

How is performance measured over time and does it improve with new models? Answer: cases, data, results and queries are stored; a new model is back-tested against known cases and playbooks, and questioned if it misses known results or costs too much.

How would this scale toward autonomous defense or write ability? Answer: run it as a non-human identity around the clock with a 10-minute tick in manageable batches to avoid alert-storm cost; write ability not pursued, and a human stays in the loop for likely true positives.
What is the feedback loop for false positives and negatives? Answer: how many times an analyst has to steer or correct it, plus changes to the production instance via reviewed pull requests.

Why an interactive harness, and what would an ambient one need? Answer: depends on the case; fully autonomous only with near-100 percent confidence such as false positives, otherwise a human verifies and joins any resulting incident.

key_frames.caption: How Ultron was built: Alfred (spine) plus Friday (brain) merged, with the design chips including GET-only chokepoint and CI containment test.
How it runs: operator, 10-minute tick, investigation core with CONFIRMED/DEDUCED/UNKNOWN, evidence bus, local state and human-gated controls.
Indicator-based routing table and the four routing rules, including that egress never settles location.
Trust boundary: read-only by construction, ask-then-deny, cited claims, scorecard against analysts.
Evidence table separating spoofable network egress from confirmed device, HR and physical-plane evidence.

signal.reason: The talk shows a design pattern (read-only by construction, source-health preflight, cited claims, indicator routing) in detailed slides and a replayed fictional case, with no production metrics presented.

caveats: The captions say traffic travelled about 10,000 km; the masking slide says about 9,000 km, and this record uses the slide.
The captions say Wi-Fi radios indicate the country; the slide gives the regulatory country code as XL, and this record uses the slide.
The embedded demo video shows only its first two minutes legibly in the recording; the later physical-plane steps rely on the narration and the summary slides.
Q&A timestamps are approximate because the transcript has a gap between 17:35 and 18:08.
The conference Q&A slide shows a venue Wi-Fi credential, which is deliberately not recorded here.
